title: Stock Span
directAnswer: The span at day i is how many consecutive days back (including today) the price was ≤ today's price. Brute force walks backward each day for O(n²). The optimal keeps a monotonic decreasing stack of (price, span): pop every day whose price ≤ today, absorbing their spans, then today's span is 1 + the popped spans. O(n) amortized.

remember.pattern: Monotonic decreasing stack storing (price, span); previous-greater-element in disguise
remember.formula:
span = 1
while stack and stack.top.price <= today:
    span += stack.pop().span
stack.push((today, span))
rules: Span counts back to (and stops at) the first **strictly greater** previous price. Use `<=` when popping so equal prices are absorbed into today's span.
Store the **span** (count), not the index, on the stack — popping absorbs the popped element's whole span in one move, which is what makes it O(n).
The stack stays **monotonically decreasing** in price; that invariant is why each element is pushed and popped at most once.
Span is always at least `1` (today itself counts). Initialize `span = 1` before popping.
Equivalently: `span = i − (index of previous strictly greater element)`. The (price, span) form avoids storing indices but means the same thing.
whenToUse: Online/streaming: spans must be reported as each new price arrives
'How far back until a value larger than the current one' — previous greater element
Any nearest-greater / nearest-smaller scan reducible to a monotonic stack
When a naive backward scan per element is O(n²) and you need O(n)
antiSignals: You need the next greater element to the right → still a monotonic stack, but scan direction/comparison flips
You need spans only once over a static array → a prev-greater index array is equivalent and maybe clearer
The condition isn't 'greater/smaller' but arbitrary → a stack may not apply
remember.takeaway: Stock span is the streaming face of 'previous greater element'. The monotonic stack works because once a day is dominated by a taller later day, it can never be the answer again — so you pop it for good and absorb its span, giving amortized O(1) per day.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize 'count back to the previous greater price' as a monotonic-stack problem and store spans (not indices) so each element is touched once for amortized O(n).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Re-scanning backward each day (O(n²)), using strict < so equal prices break the count, or storing indices and then re-deriving spans awkwardly.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name it as previous-greater-element, prove the O(n) amortization (each element pushed/popped once), and handle the streaming variant where prices arrive one at a time.

problemStatement:
The span of a stock's price on day `i` is the maximum number of consecutive days (ending on day `i`, counting day `i`) for which the price was less than or equal to the price on day `i`.

Given the daily prices, return the span for each day. In the streaming version, return each span as its price arrives.
constraints: Span values are in [1, i + 1] for day i
understanding: For each day, count backward over the run of days whose price didn't exceed today's, stopping at the first day with a strictly higher price. The challenge is doing this without an O(n²) backward rescan per day.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are equal prices included in the span?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — the definition is 'less than or equal', so consecutive equal-or-lower days count. I pop on <= so equals are absorbed.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is this a one-shot array or a stream?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If prices arrive one at a time (the classic 'StockSpanner' design), I keep a stack across calls and return each span on arrival. The core logic is identical.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the span include today?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — today always counts, so the minimum span is 1. I initialize span to 1 before popping.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Any ties on the very first day?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Day 0 always has span 1 (no earlier days). The stack starts empty, so no pops happen.

examples.explanation: Day 5 (75): 75 ≥ 60,70,60 going back until 80 > 75 stops it → span 4. Day 6 (85): 85 ≥ 75,60,70,60,80 until 100 > 85 → span 6.
Strictly increasing — each day's price beats all previous, so spans grow 1,2,3,4.
Strictly decreasing — each day is lower than the previous, so every span is just 1.

approaches.name: Backward Rescan Per Day (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: State it to anchor the definition, then point out the O(n²) blowup on increasing prices and optimize.
hints: The span is just 'how many days back was the price still ≤ today before someone beat it'. What's the most direct way to count that?
For each day i, walk backward while prices[j] <= prices[i], counting days, and stop at the first strictly greater price.
On an increasing sequence each day rescans everything before it — that's 1 + 2 + … + n = O(n²). Can you avoid rescanning days you've already resolved?
approaches.complexityReasoning: For day i the backward walk can traverse up to i prior days. Summed over all i this is n(n+1)/2 → O(n²). Only a counter is stored beyond the output.
approaches.explanation:
For each day, walk backward over previous days while their price is `≤` today's, counting as you go, and stop at the first day with a strictly higher price.

**Why it directly encodes the definition.** The span literally *is* the length of the backward run of `≤`-priced days, so the backward loop is a faithful translation. Run it on the sample and it produces the right spans — useful as a correctness oracle.

**Why it degrades to O(n²).** Consider strictly increasing prices `[10, 20, 30, 40]`. Day 3 rescans days 2, 1, 0; day 2 rescans 1, 0; and so on — the backward walks add up to `n(n−1)/2`. For `n = 10⁵` that's ~`5 × 10⁹` steps, far too slow.

**The redundancy that points to the fix.** When day 5's price absorbs day 4, it already 'knows' how far day 4 reached back. The backward rescan throws that knowledge away and re-walks it. If each day instead recorded *its own span*, a later taller day could swallow that whole run in a single step instead of re-counting it. That memo — carry the span and absorb it — is exactly the monotonic stack.
approaches.insight: The brute force re-walks runs it has already measured. Realizing that a day, once dominated by a taller later day, will never be an answer again — and that you can absorb its precomputed span in one jump — is the leap to O(n).

dryRun.intro: For each day, count backward while price <= today's.

code.python:
def stock_span(self, prices: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(prices)
    span = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        count = 1
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and prices[j] <= prices[i]:
            count += 1
            j -= 1
        span[i] = count
    return span

approaches.name: Monotonic Decreasing Stack (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'previous greater element via a monotonic stack, storing spans so we absorb runs in one pop'.
hints: When today's price dominates several recent days, those days can never be the 'stopping point' for any future day either. What can you do with them permanently?
Keep a stack of days in decreasing price order. For each new price, pop every day whose price is ≤ today and add up their spans.
Push (price, accumulatedSpan) where the span is 1 plus the spans of everyone you just popped. Each element is pushed once and popped at most once → O(n) total.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each price is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the whole run, so the total number of stack operations is at most 2n → O(n) amortized, even though a single day's pop loop can be long. The stack holds up to n entries → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain a stack of `(price, span)` pairs kept in strictly decreasing price order from bottom to top. For each new day, start `span = 1`, then while the stack's top price is `≤` today's price, pop it and add its stored span to today's. Push `(todayPrice, span)`; that `span` is the answer for today.

**Why the stack is monotonic and what it represents.** From bottom to top the stack holds the 'candidate stoppers' — earlier days with strictly higher prices that could halt a future span, each paired with the span it accumulated. Any day whose price is `≤` a later day is dominated: it can never be the first *greater* price for anything that comes after, so it's removed permanently. That removal keeps the stack decreasing.

**Why we store the span, not just the price.** When today pops day `k`, day `k` had already counted its own backward run (its span). Today's run extends *through* day `k`'s entire run in one shot, so adding day `k`'s span — rather than re-walking those days — is what collapses the work. After popping all `≤` days, `span` equals `1 (today) + sum of absorbed spans`, which is precisely the distance back to the first strictly greater price.

**Why `≤` and not `<` when popping.** The definition counts days with price *less than or equal* to today. So an equal-priced earlier day must be absorbed into today's span, which means you pop on `≤`. Use strict `<` and equal prices wrongly halt the span, undercounting.

**Why it's O(n) amortized.** A single day might pop many entries, tempting you to call it O(n²). But each price is pushed exactly once and can be popped at most once in its lifetime — once gone, it never returns. So across all `n` days the total pop count is bounded by `n`. Total work is `O(n)`, even though individual days vary. This amortized argument is the heart of the answer.

**Why it suits streaming.** Nothing requires the full array up front. Keep the stack as state and, when a new price arrives, run the same pop-and-push to return that day's span immediately — the classic 'StockSpanner' online design.

**The equivalent index view.** `span = i − (index of previous strictly greater element)`. You could instead keep a stack of indices and a `prevGreater[]` array; the `(price, span)` formulation just folds that bookkeeping into the stack so no index arithmetic is needed.
approaches.insight: A day that's been overtaken by a taller later day is dead — it can never stop a future span — so you discard it and inherit its span. 'Discard dominated candidates, reuse their precomputed answer' is the monotonic-stack pattern shared by Daily Temperatures, Next Greater Element, and Largest Rectangle in Histogram.

pitfalls: Storing indices but forgetting to translate to spans, or using < so equal prices don't absorb.
Calling it O(n²) because one day pops a lot — it's O(n) amortized (each element popped once).

commonMistakes: Rescanning backward each day, giving O(n²).
Using strict < so equal prices wrongly stop the span.
Storing only prices and re-deriving spans instead of accumulating them on the stack.
Initializing the span at 0 instead of 1.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Strict comparison drops equal prices
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The span includes days with price ≤ today. With strict <, an equal-priced earlier day halts the span and undercounts.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while stack and stack[-1][0] < price:   # misses equal prices
    s += stack.pop()[1]
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while stack and stack[-1][0] <= price:
    s += stack.pop()[1]

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not accumulating spans on the stack
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you only store prices and pop, you lose the count of days each popped entry represented, forcing an O(n) recount per pop.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Span initialized at 0
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Today always counts toward its own span, so the base value is 1. Starting at 0 undercounts every day by one.

patternNote: Monotonic decreasing stack solving previous-greater-element, with spans accumulated on the stack so dominated days are absorbed in one pop. The reusable instinct: discard candidates that can never be the answer again and reuse their precomputed result — the engine behind Daily Temperatures, Next Greater Element, and histogram problems.
